signals.title: Position: Current Model Cards Are Insufficient for Downstream Governance of Open-Weight Foundation Models
signals.summary: The growth of open-weight foundation models (OWFMs) has prompted the AI community to re-evaluate strategies for effective downstream governance. Although model cards have been widely adopted as transparency artifacts in model repositories, existing frameworks often fail to adequately inform downstream developers and users about the distinct safety challenges posed by OWFMs.

signals.long_summary: The rise of open-weight foundation models (OWFMs) has led the AI community to reassess methods for downstream governance, highlighting shortcomings in current model cards. These model cards are utilized as transparency tools in model repositories, yet they frequently do not provide sufficient information for developers and users regarding the unique safety challenges associated with OWFMs. The inadequacies of these existing frameworks underscore the need for improved governance strategies to navigate the complexities linked to OWFMs effectively. This evolving discussion is crucial for our community, as it stresses the importance of enhancing transparency and safety to better manage the risks posed by advancing AI technologies.

signals.title: Rethinking Privileged Information in On-Policy Self-Distillation
signals.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level supervision from the same model conditioned on privileged reference information. We investigate whether performance gains from OPSD show that the student learned the information in the reference or instead reflect recovery of reasoning behavior already present in the base model.

signals.long_summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) focuses on training a student model using its own responses and token-level supervision, leveraging privileged reference information to enhance performance. The research explores whether the improvements in performance are due to the student model actually understanding the privileged information or merely reapplying existing reasoning skills that the base model already possessed. This inquiry addresses the effectiveness and implications of OPSD in developing AI models. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for the community as it informs best practices and methodologies for effective AI training and development.

signals.title: Position: AI Leaderboards Are Underserving the Global South: A Case Study from India
signals.summary: This position paper argues that AI leaderboards are structurally ill-suited to serving the Global South because they lack independent governance, conflict-of-interest policies, and mechanisms for metric evolution. The barrier is not missing data; high-quality regional benchmarks already exist: IndicSUPERB, MILU, and LAHAJA for India; IrokoBench for Africa; AlGhafa for Arabic.
signals.implication: Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators. High relevance to C2A2 operations; include in next leadership brief.
signals.long_summary: The position paper discusses the shortcomings of AI leaderboards in their ability to effectively serve the Global South, particularly highlighting issues like the absence of independent governance, conflict-of-interest policies, and mechanisms for metric development. It points out that the challenge is not a lack of data, as several high-quality regional benchmarks have already been established, including IndicSUPERB, MILU, and LAHAJA in India, along with IrokoBench in Africa and AlGhafa for Arabic. These findings emphasize the need for more equitable and responsive evaluation systems in AI that can truly represent diverse regions and contexts. Understanding these structural issues is crucial for communities looking to navigate and influence the evolving landscape of AI globally.

signals.title: Self-Evolving Agents as Dynamic Graph Transformation: A Survey and New Perspective
signals.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly becoming self-evolving systems that persist across interactions, maintain memories, use tools, acquire skills, refine workflows, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make agent states structural and dynamic: entities, relations, attributes, dependencies, and execution structures change with new evidence, feedback, and environmental conditions.

signals.long_summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are evolving into self-sustaining systems that improve over time through ongoing interactions. They are capable of maintaining memories, utilizing tools, acquiring new skills, refining their workflows, and collaborating with other agents. As these agents evolve, their states become dynamic and structural—altering entities, relationships, attributes, dependencies, and execution structures in response to new evidence, feedback, and changing environmental conditions. This development in AI systems highlights the importance of understanding self-evolution for both capabilities and governance, indicating a shift in how agents can adapt and function in complex, real-world situations. Keeping up with this evolution is crucial for the community as it shapes future AI interactions and their implications for society.

signals.title: Untitled
signals.summary: I wish this weren't phrased as if "AI" were a thing. Americans might be relying more and more on chatbots/LLMs, and imagining that they are a source of information, but calling those systems "AI" I think reinforces the plausiblity of that choice rather than pushing against it.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: The author expresses concern over the terminology used to describe chatbots and large language models (LLMs), suggesting that framing these systems as "AI" misrepresents their nature. They believe that as Americans increasingly turn to these technologies for information, labeling them as AI may lend undue credibility to that reliance instead of challenging it. This perspective highlights a critical discussion in the community regarding the implications of how we define and perceive technologies often referred to as AI. Understanding these nuances is essential for the community as they navigate the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.
